title: FAKE ARTICLE: How Much Does Tuning Matter? A Comparison of Random Forest Models
text:
Random forests are commonly introduced as flexible predictive models, but introductory applications often rely on default tuning parameters. We investigate whether tuning meaningfully improves predictive performance under a range of simulated data-generating conditions.
Using repeated cross-validation, we compare models that vary the number of candidate variables considered at each split, minimum node size, and number of trees. Our results show that tuning has relatively little impact in some high-signal settings but can substantially improve performance when signal is weaker or predictors contain substantial noise.
Keywords: random forest, machine learning, simulation, cross-validation

Interested in Reviewing?
We welcome faculty members, graduate students, and qualified undergraduate students who are interested in reviewing undergraduate research in statistics and data science.
Reviewers help evaluate the quality, clarity, methodology, and contribution of submitted work. Each manuscript is reviewed by a three-person team that includes at least one faculty member and no more than one undergraduate reviewer.

title: FAKE ARTICLE: Modeling First-Year Student Success Using Logistic Regression
text:
Student persistence remains an important question for institutions of higher education. In this study, we use logistic regression to investigate the relationship between measures of academic preparation, first-semester performance, and first-year persistence.
Using an anonymized dataset of 2,418 students, we compare candidate models using cross-validation and evaluate predictive performance using ROC AUC, sensitivity, and specificity. First-semester GPA and credit completion emerge as the strongest predictors of persistence.
The results illustrate both the usefulness and limitations of predictive models in educational settings and emphasize the importance of considering ethical implications when using student-level data.
Keywords: logistic regression, education, cross-validation, predictive modeling

title: FAKE ARTICLE: Who Answers the Survey? Exploring Patterns of Nonresponse in Campus Climate Data
text:
Survey-based research relies on the assumption that respondents adequately represent the population of interest. However, differential nonresponse can introduce substantial bias.
Using data from a university campus climate survey, we compare respondent characteristics with known population characteristics and investigate post-stratification weighting as one method for reducing observed imbalances.
Our analysis illustrates why response rate alone is an incomplete measure of survey quality and highlights the importance of examining who is represented in collected data.
Keywords: survey sampling, nonresponse, weighting, missing data
